'You're here again?' Pooja asked, finding Irfan on the library steps at lunch.
'Where else? Rehan's lot said the table's full. It's always full.'
'You're still trying to sit with them?'
'I thought if I got good at football...' He shrugged. 'I'm not.'
Pooja pointed at the sketchbook on his knee. 'Is that a kingfisher?'
'Common kingfisher. I saw it at the lake on Sunday. The colours were ridiculous.'
'We've got a bird-count group. Saturdays, six in the morning, by the lake. Four of us and one pair of binoculars we fight over.'
'Six? In the morning?'
'The birds don't wait for you to wake up.' She grinned. 'Bring the sketchbook. Nobody in the group can draw.'
Irfan turned a page. 'I've got a heron too.'
'Then you're definitely coming.'
On Saturday he was at the lake at ten to six.

Last term, when my old group started sitting with the girls from 10B, I spent weeks trying to squeeze back in. I laughed at jokes I didn't get. I bought the same keychain. Nothing changed; I was still the one at the end of the bench.
Then I saw the notice: 'Backstage crew needed for annual play. No acting. Paint, glue, hammers.'
Raghav, who ran it, handed me a brush on the first day and said, 'Vidya, the forest needs more trees.' That was it. No test.
For three weeks we painted, argued about shades of green and ate samosas on dust sheets. Nobody had to be interesting. We just had to finish the forest.
I still see my old group in the corridor. It stings less now. I've got somewhere to be at four.

Uday pulled a chair up to Harsha's desk after the others had left. 'You've got that look. Up late on the phone?'
Harsha shrugged.
'When I was twenty,' Uday said, 'I did my engineering in Delhi. First time away from Mysuru. Every night I'd sit with my laptop watching videos: other people's road trips, other people's birthday parties. I told myself it was relaxing. Really I was watching everyone else have a life.

The screen lit up: Vidya calling. His sister rang every Sunday; he had missed the last three. He watched it buzz. She had her own exams, her own mess. Why add his?

Parul Ma'am closed her laptop and turned to Harish, the new analyst who ate lunch at his desk every day.
'When I was twenty-four,' she said, 'I moved to Chennai for my first job. I knew nobody. I'd go home, cook, watch something, sleep. For months.

Noor, 24, came back for a second check-in. Last month she described nights of scrolling until 2 am and feeling flatter afterwards. This time she brought a page from her notebook.
Her plan: phone apps from 8:30 to 9:30 pm, then the phone charges in the kitchen. Each week, one offline thing: a Tuesday walk with a colleague from accounts, a Sunday call with her sister in Srinagar.

She reports sleeping better, and the one walk has become two.
Next: follow-up in a month. I suggested adding a weekend plan only if she wants one.

passage:
It started with one debate round in September. I told Ma'am I had a sore throat, and the relief was so huge I nearly laughed.
By October I was letting calls go to voicemail. Not just unknown numbers, everyone. Dolma rang three times about the tuition carpool, and I texted 'got a lift' when I hadn't. I walked the forty minutes instead so I wouldn't have to talk in the car.
Then Sunday football went. Then the group chat. Each thing I dropped felt like one less danger, but the things left felt scarier. Even buying bread at the corner shop made my chest tight.
Looking back, Sahil in September would never have believed Sahil in November: a person whose safe world was basically a bedroom and a school desk.

qa.q: What excuse did Sahil give to skip the debate round?
qa.a: Sahil told Ma'am about having a sore throat.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel each time another activity was dropped?
qa.a: Each drop brought a short sense of safety, but what remained felt scarier, until even buying bread made Sahil's chest tight.

qa.q: What could have been a turning point for Sahil around October?
qa.a: Telling a parent or the school counsellor about the tight chest and the dodged calls could have led to small, supported steps back, like one carpool ride with Dolma.

qa.q: What might Dolma have been experiencing as the carpool offers kept being turned down?
qa.a: Dolma might have felt puzzled or brushed off after three calls and a 'got a lift' text, not knowing Sahil was walking forty minutes to avoid talking.

grounding: It shows avoidance spreading from one debate round to calls, carpools, football and the group chat until the safe world shrinks to a bedroom and a desk.
